abstract.p: Ovarian cancer remains a highly lethal gynecologic malignancy with limited early detection and frequent relapse. Claudin-6 (CLDN6), minimally expressed in normal tissues but frequently upregulated in ovarian cancer, represents a promising tumor-specific target. Bispecific T-cell engagers (BiTEs) effectively redirect cytotoxic T cells toward tumor cells. However, previous studies have reported that protein-based BiTEs, particularly scFv-based constructs, may encounter challenges related to protein folding, aggregation, and in vivo stability. To address these limitations, CLDN6-nanobodies were developed through our screening platform, which display cross-species reactivity to human, murine and non-human primate CLDN6. Using this binder, we constructed CLDN6 nanobody-based BiTE (CLDN6-Nb-BiTE) encoded by self-amplifying mRNA (sa-mRNA) and delivered by lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), providing a functional alternative to protein administration. The LNP-sa-mRNA formulation was stable and uniform, enabling robust CLDN6-Nb-BiTE expression, antigen-dependent cytotoxicity, and cytokine release in vitro, while sustained CLDN6-Nb-BiTE production in vivo promoted T-cell recruitment and durable tumor control without systemic toxicity. Overall, our work introduces the first CLDN6-Nb-BiTE delivered by sa-mRNA, establishing a foundation for next-generation ovarian cancer immunotherapy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Ovarian cancer is one of the most lethal gynecologic malignancies [1], with a five-year survival rate of less than 25% [2]. Owing to the absence of specific symptoms in early disease, most cases are detected at an advanced stage [3]. Standard treatment typically consists of cytoreductive surgery followed by chemotherapy, usually combining platinum-based agents with taxanes [4]. Nevertheless, 70–80% recurrence rate associated with advanced ovarian cancer often necessitates multiple rounds of surgery and chemotherapy [5], significantly increasing patient burden. These challenges highlight the pressing need for innovative therapies capable of inducing durable responses and improving overall survival [5, 6].

Claudin-6 (CLDN6), a tight junction protein of the claudin family, is largely absent in normal tissues but is aberrantly upregulated in multiple cancers, including germ cell tumors, epithelial ovarian cancer, endometrial carcinoma, gastric cancers, and non-small cell lung cancer [7–10]. Given its frequent expression in serous ovarian carcinoma, multiple therapeutic strategies targeting CLDN6 have been developed, including bispecific T cell engagers (BiTEs) [11], trispecific T cell engager (TriTE) [12], autologous chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells [13], antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) [14], radionuclide drug conjugates (RDC) [15], and bivalent antibodies that mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity [16]. Among the multiple strategies, bispecific T cell engagers (BiTEs) represent a clinically advanced T cell engager class, designed to redirect cytotoxic T cells towards tumor cells by simultaneous engagement of CD3 on T cells and tumor-associated antigens [17].

RiboMab02.1 is a CLDN6-BiTE developed by BioNTech, which is designed to redirect T cells to attack CLDN6-positive tumor cells by simultaneously binding to CLDN6 on tumor cells and CD3 on T cells [11]. However, like conventional BiTEs, RiboMab02.1 is constructed from CLDN6 single-chain variable fragments (scFvs). Previous studies have reported that BiTEs constructed from scFvs may exhibit suboptimal folding efficiency and a tendency to aggregate, which can potentially affect their biological activity and manufacturability [18]. To mitigate these effects, recent advances in antibody engineering have led to the emergence of nanobodies (Nbs or VHHs)-the smallest antigen-binding domains (~ 15 kDa)-as robust alternatives with enhanced stability, solubility, and deep tissue penetration [19, 20]. Previous studies have shown that nanobodies, due to their single-domain structure, can retain full binding functionality and exhibit high affinity toward their target molecules, highlighting their potential as versatile antibody formats for therapeutic applications [21, 22]. The clinical approval of caplacizumab marked a milestone for Nb-based therapeutics, highlighting their translational promise [23]. Building on these advances, our group developed CLDN6-specific nanobodies through our screening platform and innovatively proposed CLDN6 nanobodies based BiTE (CLDN6-Nb-BiTE) platform in our research.

The success of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) mRNA vaccines [24, 25] has begun to foster the development of mRNA vaccines against other infectious diseases and different types of cancer [26, 27]. Various mRNA therapeutics have been developed that use either non-replicating mRNA (nr-mRNA) or self-amplifying mRNA (sa-mRNA) [28]. Inspired by these approaches, the use of RNA-delivered BiTEs represents a new frontier. RNA-encoded BiTEs offer transient, controllable expression and avoid manufacturing complexities compared with conventional protein-based BiTEs [29]. BNT142, a lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-formulated nr-RNA (nr-RNA-LNP) encoding RiboMab02.1 (NCT05262530), shows potent activity against CLDN6-positive solid tumors without notable adverse effects [11]. However, conventional nr-mRNA therapeutics are constrained by their short duration of antigen expression and the relatively high doses required to elicit effective immune responses [30, 31]. In contrast, sa-mRNA provides a key advantage: its intrinsic replication mechanism enables sustained and robust protein expression [32, 33], thereby achieving comparable immunogenicity at substantially lower doses [34]. The safety and efficacy of sa-mRNA have been validated in COVID-19 vaccine applications [35], highlighting its potential as a next-generation platform for RNA-based therapeutics that amplifies transcripts in situ to augment protein expression.

Here, we report for the first generation, characterization, and sequence disclosure of CLDN6-specific nanobodies. Using this binder, we designed CLDN6-Nb-BiTE, capable of simultaneously binding two spatially distinct epitopes on CLDN6. Building on advances in sa-mRNA, we hypothesize that sa-mRNA-mediated delivery of CLDN6-Nb-BiTE can achieve potent, tumor-specific T-cell redirection while maintaining a favorable safety profile. Our study establishes a framework for harnessing sa-mRNA platforms to deliver CLDN6-Nb-BiTE, offering a promising strategy for next-generation immunotherapies against solid tumors.

sec.title: Single-cell RNA sequencing and data processing
sec.p: For single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis, publicly available human ovarian cancer scRNA-seq datasets and matched/normal ovarian tissue scRNA-seq datasets were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Specifically, ovarian cancer datasets included GSE146026, GSE158937, and GSE154600, and normal ovary dataset included GSE118127. For each dataset, the raw gene-by-cell count matrices (UMI count tables or 10x Genomics-formatted matrices as provided by the original studies) were downloaded and imported into R (v4.3.1) for downstream analyses.

For data processing, all datasets were analyzed using the Seurat R package (v4.4.0). Count matrices were first converted into Seurat objects using CreateSeuratObject. Quality control (QC) metrics were calculated for each cell, including the number of detected genes (nFeature_RNA), total UMI counts (nCount_RNA), the percentage of mitochondrial reads (percent.mt, computed based on genes matching the pattern “^MT-”), and the percentage of ribosomal reads (percent.ribo, computed based on genes matching “^RP[SL]”). QC distributions were examined using violin plots to identify outlier cells. Cells with extremely low complexity or potential multiplets were removed by applying gene/UMI-based thresholds. In our analyses, cells were typically retained if they contained > 200 detected genes and > 500 UMIs, and cells with abnormally high gene/UMI counts were excluded using dataset-adapted upper limits (e.g., upper bounds of ~ 7,500 genes and ~ 30,000–60,000 UMIs depending on the dataset) to remove likely doublets/outliers. Mitochondrial and ribosomal fractions were calculated and inspected as part of QC to ensure overall data quality.

After filtering, gene expression counts were normalized using Seurat’s NormalizeData function (LogNormalize method; scaling factor = 10,000). Highly variable genes (HVGs) were identified using FindVariableFeatures with the variance stabilizing transformation (vst) method, selecting the top 2,000 HVGs for downstream analyses. The normalized expression matrix was then scaled using ScaleData prior to dimensionality reduction. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed using RunPCA on HVGs. The optimal number of principal components (PCs) used for downstream analyses was determined by inspection of the elbow plot (ElbowPlot), and the top PCs (typically ~ 11–14 PCs) were selected for neighborhood graph construction and clustering.

For clustering and visualization, a shared nearest neighbor (SNN) graph was built using FindNeighbors with the selected PCs. Unsupervised clustering was performed using FindClusters, with the clustering resolution selected to achieve stable and biologically interpretable separation of major cell populations (a resolution around ~ 0.8 was commonly used across ovarian datasets; resolution was adjusted when necessary according to dataset complexity). Low-dimensional visualization was generated using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) via RunUMAP based on the same set of PCs. CLDN6 expression was visualized on UMAP embeddings using FeaturePlot, and group-level comparisons were displayed using violin plots (VlnPlot) when comparing tumor versus normal conditions.

When multiple samples or batches were present, Seurat integration was applied to reduce batch effects prior to joint clustering. Briefly, each sample was normalized and variable features were identified, and integration anchors were identified using FindIntegrationAnchors (commonly using dims 1:30). The integrated expression matrix was generated using IntegrateData, followed by scaling, PCA, neighbor graph construction, clustering, and UMAP visualization on the integrated assay, consistent with Seurat’s standard integration workflow.

For cell type annotation, clusters were assigned to major cell lineages based on canonical marker genes and cluster-specific markers identified by differential expression analysis. Epithelial cells were annotated based on expression of EPCAM, CDH1, and keratin genes (e.g., KRT8/KRT18/KRT19). Immune lineages were annotated using established markers (e.g., T cells by CD3D/CD3E/TRAC; B cells by MS4A1/CD79A; NK cells by NKG7/KLRD1/PRF1; myeloid populations by LST1/LYZ/C1QA/C1QB), while stromal lineages were annotated by endothelial (PECAM1/VWF) and fibroblast (COL1A1/DCN) markers. For focused analyses, epithelial subsets were extracted and analyzed separately to evaluate CLDN6 expression patterns and tumor–normal differences within the epithelial compartment.

For differential gene expression (DGE) analyses between tumor and normal epithelial cells, cells were labeled by condition and compared using Seurat’s FindMarkers with condition as the grouping variable. Volcano plots were generated using the EnhancedVolcano package (v1.20.0) based on average log2 fold change (avg_log2FC) and adjusted p-values, and CLDN6 was highlighted together with selected genes of interest.

sec.title: Cells and mice
sec.p: HEK-293T, HeLa, OV-90 and PA-1 were purchased from the American Type Culture Collection and cultured in DMEM (Gibco) or RIPM-1640 (Gibco). Cell lines were grown at 37 °C in a humid incubator with 5% CO2. Female NSG mice and female BALB/c mice aged 6–8 weeks were used in this study. They were obtained from the Model Animal Resource Information Platform of Nanjing University (Nanjing, P. R. China) and housed in the animal vivarium of the State Key Laboratory of Biotherapy at Sichuan University in a pathogen-free environment. All mouse studies were followed a protocol approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Sichuan University. Ethical approval was given by the West China Hospital of Sichuan University Laboratory Animal Ethics Committee (approval number 2018212 A).

sec.title: Antigen preparation, camel immunization and library construction
sec.p: Briefly, the CLDN6 protein were purchase from Sino Biological. A total of 1 mg of CLDN6 protein emulsified with Freund’s complete adjuvant was subcutaneously injected at multiple sites into a camel, followed by booster immunizations every two weeks for a total of four immunizations. Serum titers were monitored, and after achieving sufficient immune response, a final boost was administered. Peripheral blood (approximately 200 mL) was collected 7 days after the final boost for lymphocyte isolation.

Total RNA was extracted from peripheral blood lymphocytes using the Promega RNA extraction kit, followed immediately by cDNA synthesis with a TaKaRa reverse transcription kit (cat. no. RR036A). VHH fragments were amplified by nested PCR and cloned into the pMECS phage display vector, followed by electroporation into TG1 competent cells to construct the phage display library.

sec.title: Phage display panning and enrichment of CLDN6-specific VHHs
sec.p: After preparation, concentration, and rescue of the phage-displayed nanobody library using helper phage, biopanning against CLDN6 was performed to enrich CLDN6-specific binders. The panning procedure was conducted as follows.

First, antigen coating was performed by diluting CLDN6 protein in PBS and coating 96-well plates at 20 µg/well for the first round (10 µg/well and 5 µg/well were used for the second and third rounds, respectively). Plates were incubated overnight at 4 °C. After antigen coating, wells were washed five times with PBST (PBS containing 0.05% Tween-20). Wells were then blocked with 5% skim milk in PBS at 37 °C for 1 h, followed by three additional washes with PBST.

For incubation with recombinant phages, the phage library was diluted in 5% skim milk to a final concentration of 5 × 10¹¹ pfu/mL, and 100 µL was added per well and incubated at room temperature for 2 h. Non-bound phages were removed by intensive washing (15 times with PBST). Bound phages were eluted by adding 0.1 M triethylamine (100 µL per well) and incubating at room temperature for 10 min. The eluate was immediately neutralized with an equal volume of 1 M Tris-HCl (pH 7.4).

The remaining phage solution was used to infect TG1 cells in logarithmic growth phase. After 30 min incubation at 37 °C without shaking, 2 mL of infected culture was transferred into 8 mL 2×YT medium supplemented with ampicillin and 4% glucose and incubated at 37 °C, 220 rpm to logarithmic phase. Helper phage rescue was then performed, followed by amplification and PEG/NaCl-mediated phage concentration. The above panning procedure was repeated for a total of three rounds (Rounds 1–3), using decreasing antigen-coating amounts to increase selection stringency. Enrichment of CLDN6-specific phages was evaluated by phage titration and subsequent sequencing of positive clones.

sec.title: Preparation of sa-mRNA/nr-mRNA
sec.p: sa-mRNA/nr-mRNA constructs encoding CLDN6-Nb-BiTE or control proteins were designed using codon-optimized sequences and synthesized in vitro. Linearized plasmid DNA containing the T7 promoter and the sa-mRNA/nr-mRNA cassette served as the transcription template. In vitro transcription was performed using the T7 RNA polymerase according to the manufacturer’s instructions (cat. no. DD4201, Vazyme Biotech Co.,Ltd). Following transcription, the sa-mRNA/nr-mRNA products were treated with DNase I to remove template DNA and purified by LiCl precipitation. RNA integrity and purity were confirmed using the Qsep1 capillary electrophoresis system (BiOptic). Purified sa-mRNA was capped, aliquoted and stored at − 80 °C until further use.

sec.title: Lipid nanoparticle formulation
sec.p: Encapsulation of sa-mRNA/nr-mRNA into lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) was performed using a microfluidic mixing system. Briefly, the aqueous phase containing sa-mRNA/nr-mRNA in citrate buffer (pH 4.0) was rapidly mixed with an ethanol phase containing a lipid mixture of SM102, DSPC, cholesterol, and PEG-lipid at a molar ratio of 50:10:38.5:1.5. The aqueous-to-organic phase flow ratio was maintained at 3:1, with a total flow rate of 12 mL/min, to ensure the formation of uniformly sized nanoparticles. LNPs were subsequently dialyzed against phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) to remove ethanol and adjust the pH to physiological conditions. Particle size, polydispersity index (PDI), and zeta potential were measured using dynamic light scattering. Encapsulation efficiency of sa-mRNA was quantified by RiboGreen RNA assay (cat. no. Kit R11490, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). LNPs were stored at − 80 °C for long-term stability studies and thawed immediately before in vitro or in vivo applications.

sec.title: Nanoparticle characterization by nano-flow cytometry
sec.p: The particle concentration and sa-mRNA encapsulation efficiency of LNP formulations were assessed using a nano-flow cytometry system. Prior to measurement, the instrument was calibrated with monodisperse silica nanoparticle standards of known diameters according to the manufacturer’s instructions. LNP samples were diluted in sterile-filtered PBS to an appropriate concentration to avoid swarm detection. For RNA-loaded particle detection, LNPs were stained with SYTO™ RNASelect fluorescent dye (cat. no. S34854, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) following the manufacturer’s protocol. Data were acquired under identical instrument settings for all samples to determine particle number and size distribution based on side-scatter signals, while fluorescence detection was used to quantify RNA-positive LNPs. The sa-mRNA encapsulation efficiency was calculated as the percentage of RNA-positive particles relative to total particles, and the fraction of empty LNPs was determined based on the ratio of total particles to RNA-positive particles.

sec.title: Label-free live-cell imaging
sec.p: Label-free live-cell imaging was performed using the SC3000 live cell microscopy system (ZIRCON). Cells were seeded in appropriate culture plates and allowed to adhere overnight. During imaging, cells were maintained at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO₂ using the system’s on-stage environmental control. Time-lapse images were acquired under label-free bright-field-based imaging mode. Image acquisition and data collection were controlled by the manufacturer-provided software. Cell morphology, proliferation, and dynamic cellular responses were analyzed from time-lapse image sequences using the integrated analysis tools.

sec.title: Quantification of circulating BiTE by ELISA
sec.p: Blood samples were collected from mice at the indicated time points after treatment. Whole blood was allowed to clot at room temperature and then centrifuged at 3,000 × g for 10 min to obtain serum. The concentration of circulating CLDN6×CD3 BiTE in serum was quantified using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Briefly, serum samples were added to ELISA plates coated with the appropriate capture antibody, followed by incubation with a detection antibody and an HRP-conjugated secondary antibody. The signal was developed using TMB substrate and measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader. BiTE concentrations were calculated based on a standard curve generated using purified recombinant BiTE protein.

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry
sec.p: Tumor tissues were harvested from treated and control mice, fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin for 24 h, and embedded in paraffin. Five-micrometer sections were cut, deparaffinized in xylene, and rehydrated through a graded ethanol series. Antigen retrieval was performed using citrate buffer (10 mM, pH 6.0) in a pressure cooker for 15 min. Endogenous peroxidase activity was quenched with 3% hydrogen peroxide for 10 min. Sections were blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) for 30 min at room temperature, followed by incubation with primary antibodies targeting human/mouse CD3 or CLDN6 overnight at 4 °C. After washing, slides were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Signal was visualized using 3,3′-diaminobenzidine (DAB) substrate, and sections were counterstained with hematoxylin.

sec.title: Flow cytometry
sec.p: Single-cell suspensions were prepared from tumors or peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) using mechanical dissociation followed by filtration through a 70 μm cell strainer. Cells were washed and resuspended in PBS containing 2% FBS. For surface staining, cells were incubated with fluorophore-conjugated antibodies against human/mouse CD3, CD8, CD4, and CLDN6 for 30 min at 4 °C in the dark. Data were acquired on flow cytometer and analyzed using FlowJo V.10.8.1. The frequency of CD3⁺, CD8⁺, CD4⁺ T cells and cytokine-producing populations were quantified to assess T cell activation and tumor-targeted immune responses.

sec.title: Real-time Cytotoxicity Assays (RTCA)
sec.p: Real-time cytotoxicity assays (ACEA Bioscience, Inc. xCELLigence RTCA SP) were used to detect the ability of CAR-T cells to lyse target cells. E-plate 96 (ACEA Bioscience) was used to culture CLDN6-HeLa/OV-90 tumor cells (104 cells per well) for around 24 h before the plates were treated with PBMCs (E: T = 10). Data were gathered and examined in line with the manufacturer-specified methods (ACEA Bioscience, Inc. RTCA Software 2.1).

sec.title: Cytotoxicity assay and calculation of specific lysis
sec.p: Target cells were seeded in 96-well plates and co-cultured with effector cells under the indicated experimental conditions. After incubation for the specified period, cytotoxic activity was quantified by measuring luminescence using a luminescence-based cell viability assay according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Wells containing target cells alone served as the target-only control to define 0% lysis. Luminescence signals were recorded using a microplate reader. Specific lysis was calculated using the following formula:
Specific lysis (%) = [1 − (luminescence of experimental group / luminescence of target-only control)] × 100.

sec.title: Cytokine production assays
sec.p: Tumor cells were co-cultured with reactive cells in 24-well plates at 37 °C in the absence of exogenous cytokines. After 48 h of incubation, culture supernatants were collected and centrifuged to remove cell debris. The concentrations of IL-2, IFN-γ, and TNF-α in the supernatants were quantified using ELISA kits according to the manufacturers’ instructions. Specifically, LEGEND MAX™ Human IFN-γ ELISA Kit (cat. no. 430107), LEGEND MAX™ Human TNF-α ELISA Kit (cat. no. 430207), and LEGEND MAX™ Human IL-2 ELISA Kit (cat. no. 431807) were purchased from BioLegend (USA). Absorbance was measured using a microplate reader, and cytokine concentrations were calculated based on standard curves generated with recombinant cytokine standards provided in the kits.

sec.title: In Vivo Imaging System (IVIS)
sec.p: The mice were imaged with the IVIS using luminescent imaging by injecting intraperitoneally (i.p.) 150 mg kg− 1 of body weight D-luciferin. ROI measurements were taken through the Living Image 4.5 software.

sec.title: Graphs and statistical analysis
sec.p: Graphs were performed using GraphPad Prism Software version 8.3.0. Some of these graphs were obtained and modified from BioRender.com. All results are expressed as means ± SEM (n = 3–5) as indicated. T-test was used to compare the statistical difference between two groups, and one-way or two-way analysis of variance with Sidak’s or Tukey’s multiple comparison tests were used to compare three or more groups (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.005, ****P < 0.0001). Survival curves were generated by the Kaplan-Meier method and compared using the log rank (Mantel-Cox) test. GraphPad Prism V.8.3.0 software was used to calculate significance between the samples. FlowJo V.10.8.1 was used to analyze data of flow cytometry. All experiments were repeated, and representative figures were presented unless otherwise noted. P values ≤ 0.05 were considered significant.

sec.title: Evaluation of CLDN6 expression in ovarian cancer tissues and cell lines
sec.p: Initially, analysis of mRNA data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) was performed to identify CLDN6 as potential suitable targets for the development of antibody-based therapeutics. CLDN6 was limited to no expression in most cancers, while highly expressed in ovarian cancers and testicular cancers (Fig. 1a). Another analysis from TCGA was performed to elevate CLDN6 expression was associated with shorter disease-free survival times (Fig. 1b). Differential expression analysis was performed using six publicly available ovarian cancer transcriptome datasets (GSE154600, GSE181955, GSE130000, GSE146026, GSE158937, and GSE118127) obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. After normalization and batch correction, a set of significantly dysregulated genes was identified between ovarian cancer and normal ovarian tissues. As shown in the volcano plot, CLDN6 exhibited a positive log₂ fold change with a markedly low false discovery rate (FDR), indicating that CLDN6 expression was significantly elevated in ovarian cancer tissues compared to normal controls (Fig. 1c). To further characterize the spatial expression pattern of CLDN6 at the single-cell level, Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) visualization was conducted using integrated single-cell RNA sequencing data. CLDN6 was scarcely expressed in normal ovarian tissues but prominently expressed across multiple malignant cell clusters in ovarian cancer samples (Fig. 1d). Quantitative analysis confirmed a significant upregulation of CLDN6 in the diseased group relative to the control group (Fig. 1e). Moreover, analysis of multiple independent single-cell datasets (GSE146026, GSE158937, GSE154600, and GSE118127) revealed that CLDN6 expression was predominantly restricted to epithelial cell populations across ovarian cancer samples, while immune (T cells, macrophages, NK/T cells, B cells) and stromal (fibroblasts, endothelial, and smooth muscle) cells exhibited minimal expression (Fig. 1f). To validate the transcriptomic findings, CLDN6 expression patterns were further examined at both the tissue and transcriptome levels. Immunofluorescence staining of ovarian cancer specimens from two independent patients revealed strong CLDN6 signals (red) predominantly localized to the membranes of malignant epithelial cells, whereas surrounding stromal regions showed negligible staining (Fig. 1g). These results confirm the epithelial-specific and elevated expression of CLDN6 in ovarian cancer tissues. Analysis of RNA expression data from TCGA further supported these observations. In normal tissues, CLDN6 expression was extremely low, indicating restricted physiological distribution (Fig. 1h). In contrast, CLDN6 expression was markedly elevated across ovarian cancer samples, with particularly high transcript levels detected in specific tumor subtypes (Fig. 1i). Together, these results consistently demonstrate that CLDN6 is selectively overexpressed in ovarian cancer and rarely expressed in normal tissues, underscoring its potential as a tumor-specific biomarker and promising therapeutic target.

sec.title: CLDN6-VHH library construction and specific nanobodies screening
sec.p: A healthy 3-year-old camel was immunized through the subcutaneous route following previously reported procedures (Fig. 2a) [36]. After the third immunization, immunological titers were determined (Fig. 2b), and peripheral blood lymphocytes were isolated from 200 mL of fresh blood by density-gradient centrifugation. Total RNA was extracted from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and reverse-transcribed into cDNA using the SuperScript III First-Strand Synthesis System (Thermo Fisher, USA). The VHH genes were then amplified, cloned into the pMECS phagemid vector, and transformed into E. coli TG1 competent cells (Fig. 2a). Three rounds of biopanning were subsequently performed to enrich for specific nanobodies, with the screening progress monitored by polyclonal phage enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (Fig. 2c). Positive clones were identified by monoclonal phage ELISA, and randomly selected colonies were sequenced to evaluate library diversity (Fig. 2d). This systematic screening ultimately yielded two distinct nanobodies against CLDN6, distinguished by unique amino-acid compositions within their complementarity-determining regions (sequences were shown in Table S1).

sec.title: Characterization of the CLDN6 nanobodies
sec.p: To further characterize the binding properties of CLDN6-Nb-1 and CLDN6-Nb-2, Nbs-hFc were constructed, expressed, and purified as illustrated in the Figure S1. Specific binding to CLDN6 was confirmed by immunofluorescence analysis (Fig. 2e). Consistently, flow cytometry demonstrated that both Nbs-hFc recognized human, mouse and cynomolgus monkey CLDN6 (Fig. 2f; sequences were shown in Table S2). The binding of nanobodies to I143V-mutated CLDN6 was also confirmed (Figure S2a, b), which is a major single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) of human CLDN6 (CLDN6 (SNP)). Competition binding experiments were performed to demonstrate that the two anti-CLDN6 Nbs do not compete with each other for binding and can bind simultaneously, supporting the conclusion that they recognize different epitopes on CLDN6 (Figure S2c).

Next, the epitopes recognized by the two nanobodies were systematically investigated. Given the high sequence similarity between CLDN6 and its paralog CLDN9, chimeric constructs were generated by substituting each extracellular loop of CLDN9 with the corresponding region of CLDN6. Flow cytometric analysis revealed that both nanobodies retained binding activity when the second extracellular loop (ECL2) of CLDN6 was preserved, indicating that their epitopes are located within or dependent on ECL2 (Fig. 2g; detailed mean fluorescence intensity values are provided in Table S3). Based on our mapping results indicating the importance of the ECL2 region for binding, we expressed this extracellular loop on the cell surface and tested nanobody recognition. Unfortunately, both nanobodies failed to bind to the isolated ECL2 fragment, indicating that they recognize conformational rather than linear epitopes (Figure S3). Sequence alignment between CLDN6 and CLDN9 identified two amino acid differences within ECL2 (R145 and Q156 in CLDN6 versus Q and L in CLDN9) (sequences were shown in Table S4). To validate their contribution to nanobody recognition, we introduced point mutations (R145Q and/or Q156L) into CLDN6. Flow cytometry showed that the R145Q mutation markedly impaired CLDN6-Nb-2 binding, whereas CLDN6-Nb-1 binding remained unaffected even in the double mutant (Fig. 2h). These findings indicate that CLDN6-Nb-1 and CLDN6-Nb-2 target distinct epitopes on CLDN6. Considering binding affinity and potential off-target effects, we subsequently designed a biparatopic nanobody tandem targeting both epitopes (Figure S1). Moreover, confocal imaging confirmed that the biparatopic nanobody tandem selectively bound CLDN6 without cross-reactivity to closely related family members CLDN3, CLDN4, or CLDN9 (sequences were shown in Table S5), underscoring its high binding specificity (Fig. 2i). Collectively, these results illustrate the generation and precise epitope characterization of two non-overlapping CLDN6-specific nanobodies and the design of a biparatopic construct with high binding specificity.

To further support the binding characteristics of our constructs, flow cytometry-based binding assays and immunofluorescence assays were performed to demonstrate concentration-dependent binding of CLDN6 Nb/scFv-based constructs to CLDN6-expressing target cells (Figure S4, S5). We also evaluated the stability of the CLDN6 Nb/scFv-based constructs under stress-related conditions and compared their performance accordingly (Figure S6). These data were included to assess the intrinsic biophysical robustness of the antibody component itself, independent of delivery format or expression platform. Besides, the biparatopic format demonstrated improved tumor cell killing compared with the monospecific construct, although the mechanistic basis for this observation remains unclear. (Figure S7). Based on this functional difference, subsequent experiments were focused on the biparatopic construct as the lead candidate, and the monospecific CLDN6×CD3 was therefore not included in all downstream efficacy studies.

sec.title: sa-mRNA generation and LNP characteristics
sec.p: As shown in Fig. 3a, the schematic depicts the structural organization of the sa-mRNA. The non-structural proteins correspond to the replicase region derived from the TC-83 strain of Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV), which subsequently drives intracellular self-amplification of the sa-mRNA (see Table S6 for detailed sequence information). The in vitro transcribed sa-mRNA remained intact after storage at − 80 °C, demonstrating excellent RNA stability (Fig. 3b, c). Using a microfluidic mixing system, sa-mRNA was encapsulated into LNPs via electrostatic interactions between the negatively charged RNA backbone and the cationic lipid SM-102 (Fig. 3d). The resulting formulations were dialyzed and stored at − 80 °C for one month. Both freshly prepared and stored LNPs exhibited a distinct Tyndall effect under UV illumination (Fig. 3e). The Tyndall effect refers to the visible scattering of light by colloidal nanoparticles in suspension, resulting in a bright light path when illuminated, which indicates successful nanoparticle formation and dispersion.

Comprehensive physicochemical characterization was performed by dynamic light scattering (DLS), nano-flow cytometry, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and zeta potential and encapsulation efficiency measurements. The zeta potential of freshly prepared sa-mRNA–LNPs (8.64 ± 6.06 mV) was comparable to that of LNPs stored at − 80 °C (10.74 ± 4.86 mV) (Fig. 3f). Nano-flow cytometry analysis revealed particle concentrations of 8.6 × 10¹²–14.9 × 10¹² particles/mL for freshly prepared LNPs and 8.8 × 10¹²–13.9 × 10¹² particles/mL after storage (Fig. 3g). Both maintaining encapsulation efficiencies above 90% (Fig. 3h). DLS measurements showed mean particle diameters of 106.4 ± 8.2 nm for freshly prepared and 107.6 ± 9.9 nm for stored formulations, with consistent polydispersity indices (0.166 ± 0.02 and 0.164 ± 0.03, respectively) (Fig. 3i-k). SYTO-9 staining followed by nano-flow cytometry revealed that approximately 30% of LNPs were empty (Fig. 3l). TEM imaging confirmed that both preparations retained a well-defined spherical morphology (Fig. 3m). Together, these results demonstrate the successful encapsulation, high stability, and uniform morphology of sa-mRNA-LNPs during storage at − 80 °C. Next, Cy5-labeled sa-mRNA was conducted to assess intracellular trafficking of LNP-delivered sa-mRNA by the SC3000 live cell microscopy system (Figure S8). Robust intracellular Cy5 signals confirmed efficient cellular uptake of LNP-sa-mRNA. Notably, the sa-mRNA signal showed only partial colocalization with endosomal markers, consistent with endosomal escape following internalization.

sec.title: Cytotoxicity of CLDN6-Nb-BiTE sa-mRNA in vitro
sec.p: To verify the in vitro stability and functionality of the proteins encoded by sa-mRNA, a series of sa-mRNA constructs were generated, as illustrated in the Fig. 4a. These constructs encoded enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP), bispecific T cell engager engineered from CLDN6 nanobodies recognizing distinct epitopes of CLDN6 (CLDN6-Nb-BiTE), and a corresponding control bispecific T cell engager (CONTROL-Nb-BiTE). Sequence information of the anti-human/anti-mouse CD3 scFv was shown in Table S7.

Notably, human embryonic kidney (HEK)-293T cells transfected with LNP-formulated eGFP-encoding sa-mRNA exhibited sustained and high-level expression for at least seven days after transfection (Fig. 4b). The cytotoxicity of LNP-formulated CLDN6-Nb-BiTE encoding sa-mRNA was directly evaluated through a co-culture experiment involving effector PBMCs and CLDN6+ cancer cell lines (CLDN6-HeLa, OV-90) at an effector-to-target (E: T) ratio of 10: 1. To evaluate cytotoxic activity, CLDN6-Nb-BiTE was tested in two formats. The first involved harvesting CLDN6-Nb-BiTE protein from the supernatant of HEK-293T cells transfected with LNP-formulated CLDN6-Nb-BiTE-encoding sa-mRNA, while the second employed direct addition of LNP-formulated CLDN6-Nb-BiTE-encoding sa-mRNA into PBMC-tumor cell co-cultures, aiming to more closely mimic the in vivo conditions following sa-mRNA administration. Subsequent to the introduction of CLDN6-HeLa/OV-90 cells into the E-Plate, the real-time dynamic alterations of the co-cultured cells were monitored using the real-time cytotoxicity assays (RTCA, xCELLigence) system. The CLDN6-Nb-BiTE protein was expressed with C-terminal His tag and purified using Ni²⁺-affinity chromatography. After binding to the nickel column, the construct was washed to remove nonspecifically bound proteins and subsequently eluted with imidazole-containing buffer. As shown by RTCA, the addition of CLDN6-Nb-BiTE protein collected from 293T supernatant induced rapid cytotoxic effects upon co-culture (Fig. 4c, d). In contrast, when LNP-formulated CLDN6-Nb-BiTE-encoding sa-mRNA was added directly, cytotoxic activity gradually emerged between 10 and 16 h post-transfection (Fig. 4e, f).

To further confirm the cytotoxicity of LNP-formulated CLDN6-Nb-BiTE-encoding sa-mRNA transfection, stable luciferase (Luc)-expression cell lines were generated from CLDN6-HeLa, OV-90 and PA-1 cell lines to perform luciferase-based determination of cytotoxicity. CLDN6-HeLa, OV-90 and PA-1 cells were efficiently lysed following 72 h of co-culture (Fig. 4g). Cytokines were measured during the in vitro cytotoxicity assay. In the LNP-formulated CLDN6-Nb-BiTE-encoding sa-mRNA administration group, increased expression of effector cytokines such as interleukin-2 (IL-2), interferon-γ (IFN-γ) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) when PBMCs co-cultured with CLDN6+ target cells (CLDN6-HeLa, PA-1, OV-90), while produced few or no cytokines when co-cultured with CLDN6– target cells (Fig. 4h-j). Together, these results demonstrate that LNP-formulated CLDN6-Nb-BiTE sa-mRNA enables effective in vitro protein expression, induces potent and selective cytotoxicity against CLDN6+ cancer cells, and promotes antigen-dependent cytokine release.

sec.title: Evaluation of the translatability and organ toxicity of sa-mRNA and nr-mRNA in vivo
sec.p: As shown in Figure S9a, the schematic depicts the structural organization of the nr-mRNA. The integrity of the RNA and its in vitro functionality after encapsulation into LNPs were confirmed (Figure S9b-d). Before the tumor treatment studies, the in vivo expression properties of the various mRNA platforms were evaluated. A series of sa-mRNA constructs were generated, as illustrated in the Figure S10. These constructs encoded Luc, mouse-derived bispecific T cell engager engineered from nanobodies recognizing distinct epitopes of CLDN6 (CLDN6-Nb-mBiTE), and a corresponding control mouse-derived bispecific T cell engager (CONTROL-Nb-mBiTE).

Mice were intravenously injected with LNP-formulated Luc-encoding nr-mRNA and sa-mRNA (Fig. 5a). Bioluminescence imaging revealed markedly stronger and more sustained signals in the sa-mRNA-LNP group compared with the nr-mRNA–LNP group (Fig. 5b). Quantitative analysis showed that sa-mRNA-LNPs exhibited lower initial expression but maintained signal through day 7, whereas nr-mRNA-LNPs peaked early and declined sharply (Fig. 5c). Ex vivo imaging further confirmed predominant luciferase activity in the liver for both formulations (Fig. 5d). To further assess immunogenicity and tissue safety, mice were injected with control or CLDN6-targeting bispecific T cell engagers (Nb-mBiTEs) encoded by either nr-mRNA-LNP or sa-mRNA-LNP (Fig. 5e). Blood samples were collected at the indicated time points after treatment, and the circulating protein levels were quantified by ELISA (Fig. 5f). As shown in Fig. 5f, sa-mRNA is capable of sustaining Nb-BiTE expression over an extended period owing to RNA replication, whereas nr-mRNA exhibits a rapid decline in expression because it is progressively degraded without amplification. Histopathological examination of major organs, including the heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney, revealed no apparent tissue damage or inflammatory infiltration across all treatment groups (Fig. 5g). Together, these data demonstrate that sa-mRNA-LNPs mediate prolonged proteins expression in vivo without inducing overt tissue toxicity.

sec.title: CLDN6-sa-Nb-mBiTE elicits potent antitumor activity and enhances T cell infiltration in vivo
sec.p: As noted in Fig. 2f, CLDN6-nanobodies are capable of recognizing CLDN6 across human, mouse and cynomolgus monkey. Therefore, before performing in vivo antitumor studies in mice, it was necessary to identify a suitable murine tumor cell line to enable experiments in immunocompetent mice. CLDN6 surface expression on CT26 tumor cells were examined (Figure S11a) and the binding capacity of the CLDN6 nanobody to CT26 cells were confirmed (Figure S11b) to validate the suitability of this model for studies in immunocompetent mice.

To evaluate the antitumor efficacy of saRNA-delivered bispecific T cell engagers, mice bearing subcutaneous CT26 tumors were treated intravenously with either control or CLDN6-targeting Nb-mBiTEs encoded by nr-mRNA-LNPs or sa-mRNA-LNPs (CONTROL-nr-Nb-mBiTE, CONTROL-sa-Nb-mBiTE, CLDN6-nr-Nb-mBiTE, CLDN6-sa-Nb-mBiTE) (Fig. 6a). Tumor growth curves revealed that while PBS and control Nb-BiTE groups showed progressive tumor expansion, treatment with CLDN6-sa-Nb-mBiTE markedly suppressed tumor growth, whereas CLDN6-nr-Nb-mBiTE exhibited a moderate inhibitory effect (Fig. 6b, c). Consistent with these findings, CLDN6-sa-Nb-mBiTE treatment significantly prolonged overall survival compared with all other groups (Fig. 6d).

Single-cell suspensions were prepared from freshly isolated spleens and stained with viability dye and antibodies against CD3, CD4, and CD8. Flow cytometric analysis demonstrated a pronounced increase in CD3⁺CD8⁺ T cell populations in the CLDN6-sa-Nb-mBiTE group relative to controls (Fig. 6e, f). Besides, CLDN6-Nb-mBiTE treatment induces T-cell activation without apparent enrichment of regulatory or exhausted phenotypes in the CT26 mouse tumor model (Figure S12). Immunohistochemical staining further confirmed enhanced CD3⁺ T cell infiltration within tumor tissues following CLDN6-sa-Nb-mBiTE treatment (Fig. 6g, h). Together, these data indicate that sa-mRNA-encoded CLDN6-Nb-mBiTE effectively recruits and activates T cells within the tumor microenvironment, resulting in potent and durable antitumor responses.

sec.title: CLDN6-Nb-BiTE sa-mRNA treatment mediates regression of CLDN6-positive xenograft tumors in mice and prolongs survival
sec.p: To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of saRNA-delivered CLDN6-Nb-BiTE in a humanized tumor model, OV-90 ovarian cancer xenografts were established in immunodeficient mice reconstituted with human PBMCs (Fig. 7a). Flow cytometric analysis confirmed robust CLDN6 surface expression on OV-90 cells but not on CLDN6-knockout counterparts (Fig. 7b). Mice received intravenous administration of control or CLDN6-targeting Nb-BiTEs encoded by nr-mRNA-LNP or sa-mRNA-LNP at doses of 1–5 µg on days 21 and 28 post-tumor inoculation.

Tumor growth analysis revealed that CLDN6-sa-Nb-BiTE treatment led to a pronounced and dose-dependent inhibition of tumor progression compared with all other groups, whereas CLDN6-nr-Nb-BiTE showed a moderate effect (Fig. 7c, d). Consistent with the tumor growth inhibition observed at earlier time points, mice treated with CLDN6-sa-Nb-BiTE showed prolonged survival (Fig. 7e–f). However, because human PBMC-engrafted mouse models may develop graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) during extended observation, these survival data should be interpreted with caution.

Single-cell suspensions were prepared from freshly isolated spleens and stained with antibodies against CD3, CD4, and CD8. Flow cytometric assessment indicated an elevated frequency of CD3⁺CD8⁺ T cells and total CD3⁺ T cells in the CLDN6-sa-Nb-BiTE group relative to controls (Fig. 7g-i). Besides, CLDN6-Nb-BiTE treatment induces T-cell activation without apparent enrichment of regulatory or exhausted phenotypes in OV-90 ovarian cancer xenograft model (Figure S13). Moreover, the proportion of CLDN6⁺ tumor cells was markedly reduced following CLDN6-sa-Nb-BiTE treatment (Fig. 7j). Collectively, these data demonstrate that sa-mRNA-encoded CLDN6-Nb-BiTE effectively recruits and activates T cells, resulting in potent CLDN6-specific tumor eradication in vivo.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In summary, our study highlights CLDN6 as a tumor-selective antigen that is highly expressed in ovarian cancer but minimally present in normal tissues, reinforcing its value as a promising biomarker and therapeutic target. We generated and precisely characterized two CLDN6-specific nanobodies recognizing distinct non-overlapping epitopes and designed a bispecific T cell engager. The sa-mRNA-LNP formulation demonstrated excellent encapsulation efficiency, structural uniformity, and long-term stability at − 80 °C. Upon delivery, the LNP-formulated CLDN6-Nb-BiTE sa-mRNA enabled efficient in vitro protein expression, elicited potent and selective cytotoxicity against CLDN6-positive tumor cells, and induced robust antigen-dependent cytokine secretion. In vivo, the sa-mRNA-encoded CLDN6-Nb-BiTE achieved sustained protein expression and effective T cell recruitment within the tumor microenvironment, leading to durable antitumor efficacy without overt systemic toxicity. Collectively, these findings establish CLDN6-Nb-BiTE sa-mRNA as a potent and safe immunotherapeutic strategy for treating CLDN6-positive ovarian cancer.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Ovarian cancer remains one of the most lethal gynecologic malignancies, largely due to the lack of effective targeted therapies and the immunosuppressive nature of its tumor microenvironment [4]. Here, we report a sa-mRNA-encoded CLDN6-Nb-BiTE that targets two distinct CLDN6 epitopes, combining tumor-specific T cell redirection with sustained in situ protein production. Our results show that sa-mRNA-encoded CLDN6-Nb-BiTE mediates efficient in situ synthesis of functional bispecific proteins, driving potent and antigen-restricted cytotoxicity against CLDN6-positive tumor cells in vitro and in vivo. Unlike conventional recombinant BiTEs that exhibit rapid clearance and necessitate continuous infusion [37], the sa-mRNA platform enables sustained protein expression following a single administration, leading to durable immune activation. This observation is consistent with prior reports demonstrating the extended kinetics and enhanced immunogenicity of sa-mRNA therapeutics at reduced doses [34].

Importantly, our CLDN6 nanobodies recognize native murine CLDN6, allowing us to offer this CT26 system as an additional example. In that case, we also noted that tumor control in the reconstructed human CLDN6-expressing mouse model was less robust than in the CT26 model that endogenously expresses murine CLDN6. This difference is expected, as endogenous antigen expression more faithfully reflects physiological regulation and antigen density. Although the PBMC-humanized NSG mouse model offers a valuable system for evaluating the in vivo activity of human T cell-redirecting agents, it is inherently limited by the occurrence of GVHD due to species-related major histocompatibility complex mismatch [38]. Similar to prior observations [11], GVHD development in this model complicates long-term survival analysis and obscures clear assessment of dose dependency. Nonetheless, the observed survival benefit in our treated cohorts primarily reflects tumor control rather than GVHD onset, as control animals reached ethical endpoints owing to tumor burden, whereas most treated animals were euthanized upon GVHD manifestation or at study termination. Together, these data demonstrate that sa-mRNA-encoded BiTEs can effectively reshape the tumor immune microenvironment and elicit durable antitumor immunity with a favorable safety margin.

Lipid nanoparticles have become the most clinically advanced nanocarrier system for nucleic acid delivery, with multiple approved formulations and extensive clinical experience supporting their translational potential [39]. The widespread deployment of mRNA-LNP vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic further demonstrated their scalability, manufacturing robustness, and ability to elicit potent biological responses in humans [40]. However, despite these advantages, LNPs-as well as other synthetic nanocarriers-largely rely on passive biodistribution following systemic administration [41]. Consequently, they preferentially accumulate in highly perfused or clearance-associated organs such as the liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys, which may limit their effectiveness for indications requiring precise tissue or cell-type targeting and may also raise safety considerations for immunostimulatory payloads [42]. Alternative nanocarrier platforms, including polymer-based nanoparticles and extracellular vesicles (EVs), have been explored to address these limitations. Polymeric nanoparticles offer chemical tunability and structural stability but often suffer from suboptimal cytosolic delivery efficiency and limited clinical translation. EVs, by contrast, are endogenous vesicles involved in intercellular communication and have attracted interest due to their potential intrinsic tissue-homing properties [43]. Nevertheless, the clinical development of EV-based delivery systems remains challenging because of their compositional heterogeneity, incomplete mechanistic understanding, and difficulties in large-scale, standardized manufacturing and regulatory approval [44]. In this context, the sa-mRNA/LNP platform represents a pragmatic compromise between translational maturity and therapeutic versatility, enabling sustained in situ expression of complex immunotherapeutics such as BiTEs. At the same time, the prolonged expression enabled by sa-mRNA may amplify immune-related risks, underscoring the importance of future head-to-head comparisons with alternative nanocarriers to optimize both efficacy and safety for cancer immunotherapy applications.

Despite the encouraging antitumor efficacy and favorable histopathological findings observed in this study, several safety considerations specific to both the sa-mRNA/LNP platform and the BiTE therapeutic class warrant further investigation. In particular, immunogenicity associated with LNP components (e.g., anti-PEG antibodies) or with repeated sa-mRNA administration was not systematically evaluated here and may influence durability of response upon redosing. Likewise, while in vitro T-cell activation assays suggested controlled immune engagement, longitudinal in vivo monitoring of systemic cytokines was not performed, precluding a comprehensive assessment of cytokine release syndrome risk. In addition, although CLDN6 is considered largely tumor-restricted, more sensitive analyses of potential on-target, off-tumor effects in low-expressing normal tissues will be essential in future studies. Finally, although CLDN6-Nb-BiTE treatment induces T-cell activation without apparent enrichment of regulatory or exhausted phenotypes, these observations were obtained from a relatively small cohort and should be further validated in larger studies. Future work will therefore include dedicated safety and toxicology studies incorporating serial cytokine profiling, immunogenicity assessments, expanded organ-level evaluations, and validation in larger experimental cohorts.

Notably, our data also highlight both the promise and the limitations of BiTE monotherapy. Although CLDN6-Nb-BiTE effectively redirected T cells to eliminate tumor cells, its therapeutic impact may be constrained by the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which hampers the establishment of long-term immune memory. Furthermore, tumor heterogeneity and antigen escape remain critical challenges that can limit the durability of BiTE-mediated responses. These observations prompted us to consider a rational combinatorial approach that integrates the sa-mRNA-encoded BiTE with vaccination. sa-mRNA vaccines offer sustained antigen expression at low doses and can continuously stimulate and expand tumor-specific T cell populations [34]. Therefore, sa-mRNA vaccine serves as an antigen reservoir, maintaining systemic immune activation, while the CLDN6-Nb-BiTE functions as a targeted recruiter, guiding these activated T cells precisely to the tumor site.

Overall, our study provides a proof of concept that sa-mRNA delivery of nanobody-based bispecific T cell engagers represents a safe, potent, and programmable therapeutic approach for CLDN6-positive ovarian cancer and potentially other solid tumors.
